newsitem.title: FRANCE: $85 mln facelift for Beaubourg centre in Paris.
newsitem.headline: $85 mln facelift for Beaubourg centre in Paris.

text.p: France will spend $85 million on a millennium facelift that will partly close Paris's futuristic Beaubourg arts centre, worn out by hordes of visitors after just 20 years, officials said on Thursday.

The centre is the latest modern monument in France to show premature signs of age. Nets have been hung on the facade of the 1989 Bastille Opera to catch falling masonry. Marble on the cube-shaped Grande Arche office block at La Defense is cracking.

The two-year renovation at the Beaubourg -- sometimes known as the Pompidou Centre -- will extend the exhibition area for modern art by evicting administrative offices and include installation of a new Centre of Contemporary Creation. It will last from January 1998 until the reopening on December 31, 1999.

The long-planned facelift "is essential for the centre, for its public, for its environment, for the cultural influence of our country," Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy told a news conference outlining the long-planned partial closure.
"The centre, a symbol of modernity, could not be silent at the change of century," he said.
The renovation will cost 440 million francs ($85 million) with an extra 350 million francs on related work, some of it begun in 1992.

During the refurbishment a limited exhibition space will be kept open in the five-storey building, which shocked many members of the public in 1977 with its bright-coloured pipes and escalator bolted on the outside to create airiness indoors.
Visitors will also still be able to take the escalator up to the top for a view over Paris.

Some Beaubourg exhibitions and a public library will be temporarily housed at L'Horloge, a stone's throw away from the building in the heart of Paris. Others will travel elsewhere in France or abroad.

The Beaubourg -- designed by architects Renzo Piano of Italy and Richard Rogers of Britain -- is partly a victim of its own success. It has received 160 million visitors since it opened in 1977, more than double the original projections and an average of more than 20,000 a day.
Jean-Jacques Allaigon, president of the centre, denied that work was needed because the building was falling apart. "It's not to compensate deficiencies or fragilities of the building," he said.
But Claude Mollard, who managed the centre when it opened in 1977, said maintenance work had been virtually ignored for 20 years.

"We've waited for the centre to be worn out. The result is that we have to close the Beaubourg for two years," he told the newspaper Le Parisien. He added that visitors might lose the habit of coming after the break.

Le Parisien, reflecting on the dilapidation of many modern monuments, carried a cartoon showing two tourists looking at a poster reading: "Visit France and its heritage -- hard hat obligatory". ($1=5.106 French Franc)
